name: European NATO middle powers (2026), e.g. Spain

weightNotes.aggression: Expeditionary forces built for coalition crisis management and NATO deterrence (Spain in NATO report 2026: eastern-flank deployments, Slovakia brigade), not for initiating war; national politics are casualty-averse (Spain left Iraq in 2004). Middling-low.
weightNotes.maneuver: Trained to NATO manoeuvre doctrine (AJP-01 lineage of AirLand Battle) with professional mechanised brigades; would fight manoeuvre if they had mass, but lack depth to sustain it.
weightNotes.flanking: Same NATO manoeuvre training; middling because brigades are few and would fight inside a US- or multinational-led corps plan.
weightNotes.siegePreference: No doctrinal interest in reducing cities; urban operations only as part of stabilisation (Afghanistan, Iraq, Lebanon UNIFIL). Low.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Small armies with little depth: forces deployed forward on the eastern flank are a large share of what is ready; reserves exist mostly as low-readiness units. Educated guess.
weightNotes.scouting: Good organic ISR for their size, but RAND's Libya study (RR-676) shows European air campaigns relied on US ISR, tankers and targeting; capped at 0.6 to reflect that dependence.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Low tolerance for casualties in public and political opinion (Spain withdrew its Iraq contingent after the 2004 Madrid bombings); formations would be preserved early. Below modern breakpoints.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Professional all-arms brigades and joint training in NATO exercises; Spain fields an expeditionary amphibious group (Dedalo). Below the US because organic deep fires, air defence and EW are thin.
weightNotes.initiative: Long-service professional NCOs and officers trained in NATO mission command; Heritage (2025) calls the Spanish military 'professional and competent' despite underfunding.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: RUSI Preliminary Lessons (2022): 'no country in NATO, other than the US, has sufficient initial weapons stocks for warfighting'; with small munition stocks these forces must stay strictly inside supply and alliance logistics. High discipline by necessity.

summary: Small, all-volunteer, professional joint forces optimised since the 1990s for expeditionary coalition operations (Balkans, Afghanistan, Iraq, Libya, Mali, UNIFIL) and, since 2022, for forward deterrence on NATO's eastern flank. They fight within a NATO or US-led command structure, with modern but few platforms, good training and NATO procedures, and limited stocks, ISR and long-range fires. Spain is typical: about 2% of GDP on defence in 2026, an amphibious/carrier group, Eurofighters with stand-off missiles, and battlegroups deployed to Latvia and Slovakia.
whyItWorked: Interoperability and professionalism make them effective contributors in coalitions: the 2011 Libya air campaign was carried largely by European aircraft (RAND RR-676), and multinational battlegroups provide credible tripwire deterrence. Quality of training and equipment is high per unit.
whereItFailed: Alone they cannot fight a high-intensity war: in Libya 2011 the European-led air campaign relied on air refuelling, suppression of air defences and ISR that the United States 'predominantly contributed' (RAND RR-676); RUSI judges no European ally has the stocks or industrial capacity for sustained warfighting. Afghanistan 2001-2021 and Mali 2013-2022 ended in withdrawal without achieving their political goals, and national caveats limited what contingents could do.

sources.title: Government of Spain, Spain in NATO: An ally that delivers and leads with principles (July 2026)
